overview: Two very different fates a bacteriophage genome can choose once it gets inside a bacterial cell.
genZNote: Burn it down now, or move in quietly.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: The phage immediately hijacks the host cell to replicate, assemble new virions, and lyse the cell to release them.
aspects.valueB: The phage genome integrates into the host chromosome (as a prophage) and replicates passively along with the host, without killing it.

aspects.label: Host Cell Fate
aspects.valueA: Cell is destroyed (lysed) at the end of the cycle.
aspects.valueB: Cell survives and reproduces normally, carrying the prophage.

aspects.label: Phage Genome State
aspects.valueA: Free, actively directing production of new phage particles.
aspects.valueB: Integrated into the host chromosome, largely dormant.

aspects.label: Timeline
aspects.valueA: Fast — new virions typically released within minutes to hours.
aspects.valueB: Can persist for many bacterial generations before being induced into the lytic cycle.

aspects.label: Trigger to Switch Cycles
aspects.valueA: N/A — it is the active, destructive cycle.
aspects.valueB: Stress (UV light, chemicals) can induce the prophage to excise and enter the lytic cycle.

aspects.label: Biological Significance
aspects.valueA: Directly kills bacteria — basis for phage therapy applications.
aspects.valueB: Can confer new traits on the host via lysogenic conversion (e.g. diphtheria and botulinum toxin genes are phage-encoded).

aspects.label: Examples
aspects.valueB: Lambda phage (temperate, can choose either cycle).

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Ends in cell lysis and new virion release.
aspects.valueB: Integrates and coexists with the host without killing it.
